The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies that felt too late. Some are declarations that felt too early. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each version deleted, each version a small death of courage.

We don't talk about this, do we? The architecture of almost-said. The way words gather in the throat like water behind a dam, and how the dam holds, mostly, but sometimes—sometimes—it breaks and you find yourself crying in a grocery store parking lot because someone's song came on the radio and you suddenly need to tell your father you forgive him, or your ex that you still think about the way they laughed at their own jokes, or a stranger on the internet that their poem saved your life and you don't know their name.

I think about the messages we send and the ones we don't, and I wonder which version of us is more real. The one who speaks, or the one who retreats? The one who risks embarrassment, or the one who preserves dignity? Both feel like cowardice in different costumes.

My grandmother kept letters. Actual letters, in a cedar chest, tied with ribbon. She wrote to her sister every week for sixty years. When she died, we found them all, and I read some. They were about nothing—weather, recipes, a neighbor's dog—and everything. The texture of a life being lived in parallel, two women becoming old together through the mail. I don't know anyone who does this anymore. I don't know anyone who has a cedar chest full of correspondence. We have ephemera now. Screenshots. Voice memos we never listen to again. The illusion of permanence without the substance.

There's a message I wrote to someone three years ago. I was angry. I was hurt. I wrote seventeen paragraphs, each one more devastating than the last, each one a small masterpiece of grievance. I read it. I reread it. I felt powerful, righteous, *right*. Then I deleted it. Not because I stopped being angry. Because I realized that anger, sent, becomes a thing that exists in the world. It becomes *their* anger too. It becomes a wound that can't be unmade, only managed. And I wasn't ready to manage it. I wasn't ready to be the person who sent that message. I'm still not sure I am.

Instead, I said nothing. And nothing became its own kind of message. The silence has weight. It has shape. It sits between us like a third person at dinner, watching, judging, never speaking.

I think about this when I see people arguing in public. The couple on the subway, the friends at the restaurant, the strangers in the parking lot. They are brave, in their way. They are willing to make their conflict *real*, to let witnesses see, to risk the performance of pain. I have never been brave like that. My conflicts happen in the dark, in the space between sleep and waking, in the shower where the water is too hot and my thoughts are too loud. They resolve themselves, or they don't, but they never become *shared*. They remain mine alone, which is either a kind of privacy or a kind of prison. I can't tell which.

There's a theory that we are all writing autobiographies constantly, revising as we go, and that the self is just the story we tell ourselves about who we've been. If that's true, then the unsent messages are the footnotes we never publish. The alternative endings. The person we might have been if we'd hit send, if we'd spoken, if we'd been brave enough to let someone else read the draft.

I have a friend who sends voice notes at 3 AM. Long, rambling, unedited thoughts about her day, her fears, her hopes. She says it's easier than writing because she doesn't have to see the words, doesn't have to revise. She just speaks into the dark and sends it into the dark. I envy her. I envy the rawness, the lack of self-consciousness. I have never sent a voice note. I can't imagine my voice, unguarded, existing in someone else's phone. The vulnerability feels too exposed, too *permanent*. At least with text, I can delete. At least with text, I can pretend I was being ironic, or joking, or didn't mean it quite that way.

But voice is truth, isn't it? The voice doesn't lie. The voice carries the tremor, the pause, the catch in the throat. Maybe that's why we don't use it. Maybe we've all agreed, silently, that some things are too true to share. That intimacy requires a buffer. That we need the chance to edit ourselves into someone better, someone braver, someone who doesn't stumble over words or cry at the wrong moment or say the thing that can't be unsaid.

I think about the last message I sent to my mother. It was a photo of my breakfast. She replied with a heart emoji. We are good at this, she and I. We are good at the small, the daily, the *fine, how are you, love you*. We are not good at the large. The why. The how did it feel. The what do you think about. Those messages remain in drafts. They will probably remain there forever. She is getting older. I am getting older. The window for certain conversations narrows every year, and we both know it, and we both pretend we don't, and we send photos of breakfast and hearts and love yous, and we wait, and we hope, and we don't say the things that need saying until it's too late, or until it isn't, and we don't know which it will be.

There's a message I will never send. It's to someone who is gone. Not dead—worse, in some ways. Alive, but unreachable. The message is an inventory of everything I didn't say when I could have. Everything I thought was understood but wasn't. Everything I assumed was mutual but was only mine. I write it sometimes, in the notes app, and I read it, and I feel the old grief, fresh and clean as a wound. Then I close the app. Because what would it matter? They wouldn't read it. Or they would, and it would change nothing. Or they would, and it would change everything, and I'm not ready for everything to change. I'm not ready to be the person who sent that message. I'm not sure I ever will be.

We are all, I think, waiting to be brave. Waiting for the moment when the words will come easily, when the risk will feel worth it, when we will finally be the person we've been practicing to be. But the moment keeps moving. The person keeps changing. The drafts pile up. And we send the photos of breakfast, the hearts, the love yous, and we hope that's enough. We hope that the small things, sent consistently, add up to something like a life. Something like being known.

I don't know if they do. I don't know if anything is enough. I only know that I have forty-seven drafts in my phone, and I will probably never send them, and I will probably write forty-seven more, and the folder will grow, and someday someone will find it—my child, maybe, or a stranger who buys my phone at a yard sale—and they will read these words, these almosts, these might-have-beens, and they will wonder who I was. Who I was trying to be. Who I was afraid to become.

And maybe, in the reading, they will understand something I couldn't say. Maybe the drafts will speak for me, finally. Maybe the silence will be enough. Maybe it always was.
